explanation: No shared theme. Top hits are scattered: word pieces in the middle of words (PLA-INT-IFF, CIR-CU-IT, ins-ulators, but-anol), US state codes, numbers inside codes like T20/U11, and ordinary words ('Assets', 'reading', 'Delta', 'transferring'). Mid and weak hits are commas and function words. It cannot be predicted from the token or its context.

Mainly fires on the sport word in a player biography after a nationality adjective ('a Japanese [football] player', 'American [soccer]', 'Tonga [rugby]'). It also fires moderately to strongly on function words ('the', 'been', 'from', 'with') inside sports-news sentences about clubs, managers, injuries and suspensions. Weak or none outside sports contexts.

Money, prices and finance: words like price, pound, funds, money, afford, paid, BET, prices, per month, Finance, and function words inside financial phrases ('financed [by]', 'Bank [of]'). Strongest when the token is the money noun in a context about cost or spending. A few unrelated outliers (a YAML 'address:').

The subject pronoun that opens a methods sentence in a scientific abstract, mostly 'We' (sometimes 'They' or 'we' after a clause) followed by a research verb (we administered/examined/obtained/measured). Weak or none for pronouns in ordinary prose; a few unrelated outliers.

No clear pattern. Hits include the first digit of a year after 'in' ('in [2]013'), score digits, code tokens (link:, hibernate '.', license '-'), and ordinary nouns ('view', 'proprietary', 'home', 'fields', 'stock', 'personal'). The token cannot be predicted.

A mixture: 'presidential' in 'Democratic/Republican presidential'; the decade digit in dates written '20[1]x'; 'or'/'o' in 'one or more'/'two or more' phrases (including Spanish 'uno o más'); pieces of Japanese personal names; and assorted technical words (Metal, benefits, Security). These do not share one concept.

A capitalized 'Qu'/'qu' or 'McGu' subword at the start of a name or word (McGuire, McGuinness, Quercus, Quim, Quetta, Quarks, Spanish 'quién'/'quieren', Portuguese 'quase'), plus a few similar starts ('Cl'arence, 'Gu'imarães). Weaker on code headers (#include, https).

A noun or word that completes a fixed abstract phrase whose meaning hangs on what follows: 'key [role]', 'integral/small [part]', 'total/the [number] of', 'because [of]', 'the [only]', 'but [also]', 'in random [order]'. Fires on the head noun or preposition of these set phrases. A few code outliers.

Mostly a preposition or open parenthesis that comes right after a verb or noun and starts its complement: 'halt [by] 2015', 'appointed [by]', 'ban [for]', 'founder [in]', 'Copyright [(]C)', statistical '[(]P less than', 'increase [(]'. Opening parentheses (especially 'Copyright (') and verb-attached prepositions dominate.

A subword at the start of a word that is split into pieces, especially the Latin-prefix pieces 'ex'/'Ex'/'exc' (exploderede, EXPOSE, Explain, Examination, quasi-experimental, Gewaltexzess), 'ass'/'Ass' (assayed, Assim, ASSISTANT), 'j' (jailing, judgmental), and 'Ins'/'inter'/'cor'. Works across several languages.

Tokens inside technical or scientific compound terms and odd proper names: a word piece in the middle of a word (ep[ox]ides, amy[gd]ala, inter[cell]ular, T[GF], Dub[uis]son, Sc[ania]) or the head of a compound ('reference [signal]', 'right-eye [image]', 'growth [factor]', '6[V]'). Loosely 'completing a technical or name term'; the boundary is not sharp.

Mixed. Partly adjectives about direction or source ('external', 'foreign', 'reverse', 'backwards', 'External links'), partly contrast or negation words ('not', 'but', 'forget'), plus prepositions ('from', 'since', 'during', 'behind') and JSON values. No single rule.

Mostly the relative or interrogative word after a preposition ('in [which]', 'under [which]', 'from [which]', 'scale at [which]', 'on [what] type'), plus related words that open a restrictive clause ('those [which]', 'Errors [such] as', 'until'). The strongest hits are 'which' after a preposition. Some unrelated outliers.

Fires inside chemical names, formulas and units (positional numbers like '4,[4]-dimethyl' and '2,[2]-', 'kg[/m]2', 'gu[anine]', 'polys[il]icon', 'Mn(III[)(]', 'sodium', 'iron', 'tin'), and on subwords of some given names (Guill[ermo], Guil-ford). Mostly chemistry or units, with name fragments as a second job.

'vitro' (or 'ro' in 'in vit-ro') in the phrase 'in vitro'. Weaker for other Latin or biomedical fixed phrases and prefixes ('ad hoc', 'post'natal/'post'operative, 'prenatal', 'pre'operative, 'in situ').

The point in a Q&A or code-help post where an example or code block is introduced: 'my code[:]', 'this script[:]', 'something [like] this', 'like [this]', 'For [example]:', 'may refer [to]:', closing ``` fences and indentation inside code. Fires on the colon or introducing word just before the example.

No identifiable concept. Hits include commas inside RGB tuples and scores, '(' in license boilerplate ('or (at your option)'), 'the' after a verb, 'site', 'benefit', 'question', 'error', and postcode spaces. These are diverse function or punctuation positions with no common context.

A mixture: 'be' in GPL boilerplate ('it will [be] useful'); conjunctions or prepositions in technical lists ('Profibus [and] Modbus', 'and [the]'); subword pieces in the middle of names or medical words (pol[yc]ythemia, megal[oc]ytosis, Tr[ich]ur, N[au]voo, Cre-ighton); code tokens. No single rule.

The blank-line newline after a section heading, mainly '⏎⏎' right after a markdown 'Introduction {#...}⏎====' heading in scientific papers, just before the body text starts. Also fires on other header-to-body breaks (a dateline colon, 'First published in X⏎⏎'). Weak to moderate on ordinary sentence-final periods.

No shared feature. Hits are commas, 'to', 'of', 'we', 'want', '+' in math, '="' in HTML, 'return', 'opinion', 'bones' and 'Free' across code, legal text and prose, with nothing visible in common in the token or its context.

Mainly the capitalized first letter or letters of a proper name that is split into subwords, especially 'T' and 'G' (T-routman, T-renchard, G-raham, G-hetto, G-wyneth, G-CHQ, G-went). Also fires on the article 'a' before a noun phrase ('take [a] break', 'as [a] colonel'), which looks like a second, unrelated job.
